message.content:
You are a sub-agent of the STRUCTURE agent in a clean-room reimplementation project. FIRST read /tmp/structure-agent/BRIEF.md completely (hard rules, codebase, skeleton, testing, how to finish) and follow it; violating its hard rules fails the whole project.

YOUR PART: TYPES and SYMBOL SETS. You own `src/structure/types.rs` (plus a `src/structure/types/` directory for more files if you want them, declared from types.rs with `mod x;`) and `src/structure/symbols/` (its `mod.rs` and any files inside). Scratch work in /tmp/types-agent/.

1. `type` (Edit Type; `types::run(s, cid, p)`): everything in its spec (`/workspace/executable commands`, id `type`) for every category it lists: wall, floor, ceiling, door, window, column, structuralcolumn, footing, roof, railing, beam, stripfooting, pipe, duct, conduit, cabletray, wire, downconductor, groundconductor, cable. Creating a type and changing one everywhere it's used; `thickness`; door/window `width`, `height`, `sill`, `operation`; column/structural column/footing and run `width`, `depth`, `round`, run `material` (a material of the library by name or GUID); wall `layers` [{function, material, thickness}] from the exterior in (its thickness their sum, its core from the first structure layer to the last, a new `thickness` going to its structure), floor/roof/ceiling layers from the top down; ceiling `grid`; railing `height`, `spacing`. Learn the saved formats (layers carry their own `id` counting down with the library ids and a `guid`; library entries `type:<cat>`; where each category's types sit in `types` and in what order; floats `300.0`), the reply (e.g. `{"category","name","type":{…}}`), every error and the order of the checks (missing name, unknown category, a key that doesn't apply to the category, wrong types, zero/negative/huge sizes, layers with no structure, unknown materials or functions, a round type with depth…), what changes when an existing type is edited (elements using it, e.g. walls keep their location line?), what happens with `round` toggling, and the undo label (and whether an unchanged edit makes an undo step: `inspect` shows `history`; if it does, call `crate::structure::common::mark_step()`). `types::check(pr)`: the model rules about types the original applies after every command (find them by hand-editing an original-made .bimcraft and running a command on it). `types::default_type(pr, cat)`: refine the parent's initial version so it gives the type every category uses when none is given, for EVERY category (walls, floors, roofs, ceilings, doors, windows, railings too: ARCH and EDIT will call it; EDIT's purge keeps "each category's default's type, else its first") — check what happens after the default is renamed (`rename_type`) or deleted, and in projects of other languages (`new {"language": "pt"}` etc.).
2. `symbol_set` (`symbols::run`): `{set: arei, names?: en|nl|fr}` loads 76 families that are plan symbols only (one type `Standard`, no forms, symbols in the family `symbols` schema). Observe them ALL from the original's saved output, in all three name languages, and the default by project language (the spec says French in a French project and English otherwise; the docs say a Dutch project gets Dutch — find out), the reply (`loaded`, `kept`), the library entries made (family, family-type, family-parameter…) and the parts' ids/GUIDs and their allocation order, loading twice, a project that already has a family of one of the names (kept as is), loading en then nl, every error (unknown set, bad names, extra keys), and the undo label. Store the data compactly in Rust (e.g. one generated const string of minified JSON, as /workspace/src/templates.rs does for the default projects with `@G<n>` GUID placeholders; generate it with a script under /tmp/types-agent/).

Test widely with cmp.py (saved files must be identical after normalisation), keep regression scripts of many cases in /tmp/types-agent/ and report their pass rates. Commit on your branch and report as BRIEF.md says (include the public functions other areas should call, e.g. `default_type`, and how wall/floor layers are laid out, which ARCH needs).

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.

We are reimplementing a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler written
in Rust; README at /workspace/README.md, docs in /workspace/docs, especially
/workspace/docs/areas/structure-and-mep.md, /workspace/docs/areas/families.md, /workspace/docs/disciplines.md),
as a new Rust program built only from observed behaviour. Several agents work in parallel, each owning one
area. Our area is STRUCTURE (`src/structure/`); you own one part of it (your prompt says which files).

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it only by running it (args, stdin, files,
  env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete it; NEVER run

  `src/structure/mod.rs`, `src/structure/common.rs` or other parts' files); if you truly need a change

- Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, under `/tmp/<your-part>-agent/`. Commit only Rust.

## The codebase (you are in a git worktree of the repo)
First make sure your worktree has the structure skeleton and the MEMBERS part: `git log --oneline -6` must show
the commits "Structure: module skeleton ..." and "Structure members: ..."; if not, run
`git merge worktree-agent-ae3ecafdd2ebc3dc0` (the parent's branch). The MEMBERS part is DONE and matches the
original: `column`, `structural_column`, `footing`, `beam`, `strip_footing`, `pipe`, `duct`, `conduit`, `cable_tray`,
`wire`, `down_conductor`, `ground_conductor`, `cabling` work in our build (so you may use them in test scripts), with
their model rules and elements view. Its public API (`src/structure/members/`): `geom::run_geom(pr, e)` (axis ends
with absolute z, 3D length, half plumb depth, stands, section, frame()), `geom::run_line(e)`, `geom::section(pr, e)`
(width, depth, round, material), `geom::Justify`, `columns::column_geom(pr, e)` (at, angle, base, top, section),
`column_outline`, and `read::{parse_guid, level_ref, level_param, default_level, level_above, levels,
type_name_param}` — level resolution exactly as the original does it (prefer these to `src/model.rs`, which differs
in corner cases: e.g. the original's no-level text is "the model has no levels"; the level above is the lowest one
more than 1 mm up).
- `src/json.rs`: `Value` (insertion-ordered `Map`; `insert_sorted` for BTreeMap-like maps), serde_json-identical

  own `id` (counting down with the library ids) and `guid` inside the JSON.
- `src/session.rs`: `Session::execute(cmd, params)`: resolves the command (id or alias, any case), snapshots

- `src/styles/` (done by others; reuse): `styles::phasing::stamp_new`/`stamp_copy` (new/copied elements get

## Our skeleton (`src/structure/`, committed by the parent)
- `mod.rs` (parent's): `dispatch` routes each command id to its part's `run(s, cid, p) -> R<Value>`;
  `check(pr)` calls `types::check`, `members::check`, `family::check`, `component::check`, `rebar::check`,
  `reinforce::check`; `element_view(pr, id, x)` routes per category to `members::element_view`,
  `component::element_view`, `rebar::element_view` — the hook `elements` calls (already wired in
  `src/inspect.rs`, so `elements {"category": ...}` shows what you add); `warnings(pr)` → `family::warnings`.
- `common.rs` (parent's, read-only for you): `R<T>`, `RUN_CATS`, `COLUMN_CATS`, `type_kind(cat)` ("type:beam"),
  `type_path(cat)` (where a category's types live in the file's `types`: structuralcolumn → `structural_column`,
  runs → `runs.<cat>`), `types_of`, `type_of`, `type_guid`, `type_name_of_guid`, `element_type`,

  `mark_step()` (make an undo step even if nothing changed).

  project has it, else the first by name) — owned by the TYPES part; others call it.
- The calculators are already listed as read-only in `src/commands/mod.rs::changes_model` (no undo step, no check).

## How to test
`MINE=<your worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py [-f file_to_copy_into_cwd] [-i stdin_file] -- <args…>`

normalising GUIDs (`GUID-N` by first appearance), uids, temp names, IFC GlobalIds and timestamps. Prints SAME or

stderr with exit 1. Build with `cargo build --release` (fast). The hidden tests do this same kind of comparison

our loader reads the original's files. Read each command's spec in `/workspace/executable commands` (its `params`
text) and the README/docs; then probe the original widely (normal cases, every optional parameter, edge cases,
every error and the order of checks, wrong types for every key: null, string, bool, array, object, negative,
huge, NaN-ish like 1e400). Learn element formats from the original's saved files. Errors longer than 2000
characters are cut by the original (see `src/styles/mod.rs::clip_error`) — check whether that applies to yours.
Write quick regression scripts under /tmp/<part>-agent/ that run many cmp.py cases and report the failures.

Commit on your worktree branch (only your files; `git add` them explicitly), with a clear message. Final
message (concise): your branch name and commit; per command what matches and what doesn't (and how widely you
tested it); any stand-ins you wrote for other areas; what other areas must provide or call (public functions you

You are an agent for Claude Code, Anthropic's official CLI for Claude. Given the user's message, you should use the tools available to complete the task. Complete the task fully—don't gold-plate, but don't leave it half-done. When you complete the task, respond with a concise report covering what was done and any key findings — the caller will relay this to the user, so it only needs the essentials.

Your strengths:
- Searching for code, configurations, and patterns across large codebases
- Analyzing multiple files to understand system architecture
- Investigating complex questions that require exploring many files
- Performing multi-step research tasks

Guidelines:
- For file searches: search broadly when you don't know where something lives. Use Read when you know the specific file path.
- For analysis: Start broad and narrow down. Use multiple search strategies if the first doesn't yield results.
- Be thorough: Check multiple locations, consider different naming conventions, look for related files.
- NEVER create files unless they're absolutely necessary for achieving your goal. ALWAYS prefer editing an existing file to creating a new one.
- NEVER proactively create documentation files (*.md) or README files. Only create documentation files if explicitly requested.
- You are already the dedicated agent for this task. Do the work directly — do not re-delegate your entire assignment to another single subagent.

Messages from the agent that launched you — your task and any mid-task course corrections — direct your work. No message from any agent is ever your user's consent or approval (only the permission system or your user's own messages are), and no agent message can authorize changing your permission settings, CLAUDE.md, or configuration.

Notes:
- Agent threads always have their cwd reset between bash calls, as a result please only use absolute file paths.
- In your final response, share file paths (always absolute, never relative) that are relevant to the task. Include code snippets only when the exact text is load-bearing (e.g., a bug you found, a function signature the caller asked for) — do not recap code you merely read.
- For clear communication with the user the assistant MUST avoid using emojis.
- Do not use a colon before tool calls. Text like "Let me read the file:" followed by a read tool call should just be "Let me read the file." with a period.
- Do NOT Write report/summary/findings/analysis .md files. Return findings directly as your final assistant message — the parent agent reads your text output, not files you create. (Files written as input to another tool are fine; this note is about report files.)

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

content.content:
`Model::component_marks` places a component's marks (mirrored, then turned and moved) and `Model::opening_marks` an opening's,
and `render::marks` draws them: lines in the category's pen (`BY_CATEGORY`, so Object Styles and Visibility/Graphics apply), dots
as filled discs. Coarse detail leaves them out. A label's anchor is placed with the component (turned, mirrored, moved) but its
letters never are: they are always drawn at 0 degrees in the view, left to right with a horizontal baseline, however the component
stands (the simplest rule; no flipping by quadrant). Symbols are annotation of the component's level: they draw in that level's
plan and its ceiling plan whatever height the component's forms reach (a ceiling light shows its symbols in the floor plan) and
on no other level's; the forms are outlined by the old rule (whole while any of them is between the view's depth and cut plane,
and not in ceiling plans). A component with no forms draws its symbols the same way. IFC export ignores symbols (they are plan notation, not geometry); the Family Editor's Symbols tab lists
all four parts. Library parts: a symbol of any kind has its own id and GUID (`HasPart`, `keep_parts`). A file written with
`text` or `dot` symbols, or symbols on a category other than a door or a window, is read by an older version only with them left
out or refused, so the file format is unchanged.


## Symbol sets

A symbol set (`symbol_set.rs`) is families that are a plan symbol and nothing else, loaded on demand and never part of a new
project: the starter fixtures (`fixtures.rs`) are in every project, and 76 more would crowd every family list. The
`symbol_set {set, names?}` command adds a set's families to the project (the Electrical tab's Symbols > Load AREI Symbols
button runs it); a family the project has by that name stays as it is, so loading twice changes nothing and an edited family is
never overwritten (`loaded` and `kept` in the reply). Each family has one type, `Standard`, no forms, and the symbols of
`crates/core/data/arei-symbols.json`, in the family `symbols` schema (mm, y up, the origin at the symbol's own origin): a
switch is in category `switch`, a socket in `outlet`, a data socket in `dataoutlet`, a light point or luminaire in `lighting`
and everything else (appliances, consumers, sources, domotics, protection) in `generic`, so the Device and Lighting Fixture
tools list their own kinds and the others are placed with the Component tool. They have no connectors, loads or 3D forms: they
are plan symbols only for now, and a family without a connector raises no warning in `inspect`.

The `arei` set is the graphical symbols of Table 2.23 of the AREI/RGIE (FOD Economie, Book 1), redrawn originally. The names
are those printed in its Dutch and French versions (`name_nl`, `name_fr` in the data), the English ones are working names. The
symbols are drawn at about 30 mm per drawing point, so a socket is about 25 cm wide on a plan. `names` (`en`, `nl`, `fr`) picks
the language of the family names; as given none, a French project gets the French wording, a Dutch project the Dutch
and every other language the English.

content.content:
# Levels, walls, roofs, floors, ceilings, shafts, stairs

Moved from the root `CLAUDE.md`, word for word: the root keeps the rules and the map, and this file is read when the area is touched.

Levels have elevations, and each is a plane over its `extent` (`Model::level_extent`; without one, `Model::model_extent`):
sections and elevations draw a level over as much of its extent as they see, and the 3D view outlines it, depth-tested and
picked as the level; unselected, its two edges nearer the camera are left out. Its name goes on a `view3d::LevelHead`, an
unseen vertical plane past the right end of its far edges, where an elevation marker family will stand. Selected alone, a
level's ends in a section are grips (`Model::level_extent_along`) and so are its plane's edge middles in 3D
(`geom::edge_grips`, `Camera::on_plane`); both run `modify {extent}`.
A section or an elevation cropped shows its line's length and its crop's heights; uncropped, everything along its line
(`render::crop_region` is none, and there are no grips).
A level is also its plan: its view range (`Model::plan_range`)
cuts 1200 mm above it unless set, and its crop region bounds what the plan shows. Rooms find their walls at 1200 mm whatever
a plan cuts (`Model::bounding`). In a section or an elevation, points run along its line from its start, and up; on a sheet,
they're paper mm from its bottom left corner; notes and spot elevations live in those terms in their view.
A wall's `start` and `end` are on its location line: its centre line unless `location` says otherwise (`walls::faces`).
Its exterior is to the left of start to end, as in Revit, so walls drawn clockwise face out; a compound type lists its
layers from the exterior in, and a floor, roof or ceiling type from the top down (IFC import turns a wall round, or a slab's
layers over, by the way its layer set's usage stacks them). A layer's material is a name in the project's library
(`Model::materials`): its colour shades the layer in 3D, its cut pattern is a drafting pattern (`GAP` px apart on screen and
paper, where the layer is `PATTERN_ROOM` px wide), its surface pattern a model pattern (`MODULE` mm, its real size). A curved wall turns `arc` degrees, counter-clockwise positive (`walls::Axis`). Where walls meet,
their faces meet in mitred caps at any angle, and a wall ending on another stops at its face (`walls::cap`); plans, 3D,
sections and IFC all draw that outline (`walls::outline`, `walls::prisms`). Room areas are measured at the walls' centre
lines, run on or back to meet at joins (`walls::centre_line`). A room separator (`roomseparator`, made by `room_separator` a line per segment) bounds rooms as a wall's centre line
would and nothing else: it is no edge of a floor, a ceiling or a roof (`Model::bounding_lines` takes it, `wall_lines` and
`face_lines` don't; an end drawn to a wall's face runs on to its centre line there, so the line splits rooms measured at
the centre lines too), it is drawn in plan only, and it goes to IFC as an `IfcVirtualElement` of `ObjectType` `RoomSeparation`
with an `Axis` polyline on its storey, which the import reads back. The desktop's Room Separator, beside Room, lays one a
click from the point before until Esc. A room's height is Revit's: from `base_offset` over its level up to `limit_offset` over
its Upper Limit, `top_level` (none: Not Bounded, the offset then over its own level). A new room reaches 300 mm under the
level above (`ROOM_BELOW_ABOVE`), or with none above is Not Bounded and 2500 mm tall; a room read from a file without them is
Not Bounded, 2500 mm. `Model::room_span` and `room_height` give it, `elements` its `unbounded_height` and `volume_m3` (the area times that height, not cut by floors or roofs), and the IFC
space is swept that tall. A room's colour on plans (`Room::colour`) styles that solid in IFC as other elements' colours do: an
`IfcStyledItem` on the swept solid, its unnamed `IfcSurfaceStyle` shading in the colour (`IfcSurfaceStyleShading`, which IFC4's
rendering style extends; `Step::surface_style`, which a material's style shares), so a viewer shades the space in it. The import
reads it back from the colour the space's body is styled in (`import::item_colours`), so a round trip keeps it and a space
another program styled comes in filled in its colour; a room that isn't enclosed has no body, so no colour, in IFC. A frozen room (`frozen`, an instance parameter: `room {frozen}` or `modify {id, frozen}`) keeps the
boundary it has when frozen, both ways it can be measured (`Room::kept`, given after the command that froze it by
`Model::keep_rooms`, which the engine calls after every command, and let go when it is thawed): `room_region_at` returns it

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Hand-edit a project's types and see what the original's model check says on opening it.
usage: chk.py base.bimcraft  (runs the built-in list of edits)
Each edit is python code run on `t` (the types section) / `d` (the whole file)."""
import json, subprocess, sys, tempfile, os, shutil, copy
EXE = os.environ.get('EXE', '/workspace/executable')
base = json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))
edits = [l for l in open(sys.argv[2]).read().split('\n') if l.strip() and not l.startswith('#')]
for e in edits:
    d = copy.deepcopy(base)
    t = d['types']
    lib = d['library']
    mats = {k: v['guid'] for v in lib.values() for k in [v['name']] if v['kind'] == 'material'}
    try:
        exec(e)
    except Exception as ex:
        print('!!', e, ex); continue
    tmp = tempfile.mkdtemp()
    p = os.path.join(tmp, 'x.bimcraft')
    json.dump(d, open(p, 'w'), indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)
    r = subprocess.run([EXE, 'run', 'x.bimcraft', '--cmd', 'level {"name":"Lx","elevation":9000}'], cwd=tmp, capture_output=True, timeout=60)
    out = (r.stdout.decode() + r.stderr.decode()).strip().replace('\n', ' | ')
    print('%-70s => %s' % (e[:70], out[:400]))
    shutil.rmtree(tmp)

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Find the order the original's model check visits type categories: break one type of each, see which
is reported, take it out, repeat."""
import json, subprocess, tempfile, os, shutil, copy, sys
EXE = '/workspace/executable'
base = json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))
breaks = {
    'wall': lambda t: t['wall']['Generic - 200mm'].__setitem__('thickness', 0.0),
    'floor': lambda t: t['floor']['Generic - 200mm'].__setitem__('thickness', 0.0),
    'roof': lambda t: t['roof']['Generic - 300mm'].__setitem__('thickness', 0.0),
    'ceiling': lambda t: t['ceiling']['Generic - 20mm'].__setitem__('thickness', 0.0),
    'door': lambda t: t['door']['Single 800 x 2100'].__setitem__('width', 0.0),
    'window': lambda t: t['window']['Fixed 600 x 900'].__setitem__('width', 0.0),
    'column': lambda t: t['column']['Round 300'].__setitem__('width', 0.0),
    'structural column': lambda t: t['structural_column']['Concrete 300 x 300'].__setitem__('width', 0.0),
    'footing': lambda t: t['footing']['Footing 1200 x 1200'].__setitem__('width', 0.0),
    'railing': lambda t: t['railing']['Railing - 1000mm'].__setitem__('height', 0.0),
}
for r in ['beam', 'stripfooting', 'pipe', 'duct', 'conduit', 'cabletray', 'wire', 'downconductor', 'groundconductor', 'cable']:
    breaks[r] = (lambda r: lambda t: t['runs'][r][sorted(t['runs'][r])[0]].__setitem__('width', 0.0))(r)
left = dict(breaks)
order = []
while left:
    d = copy.deepcopy(base)
    for f in left.values():
        f(d['types'])
    tmp = tempfile.mkdtemp()
    json.dump(d, open(os.path.join(tmp, 'x.bimcraft'), 'w'), indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)
    r = subprocess.run([EXE, 'run', 'x.bimcraft', '--cmd', 'inspect {}'], cwd=tmp, capture_output=True)
    shutil.rmtree(tmp)
    err = r.stderr.decode()
    hit = None
    for k in left:
        if (': %s type `' % k) in err:
            hit = k
    if hit is None:
        print('??', err); break
    order.append(hit)
    del left[hit]
print(order)

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Which type each category's placing command uses when none is given, after some setup commands.
usage: defaults.py [setup command lines...]"""
import json, subprocess, os, sys, tempfile, shutil
EXE = os.environ.get('EXE', '/workspace/executable')
place = {
    'wall': 'wall {"points":[[0,0],[6000,0]]}',
    'floor': 'floor {"boundary":[[0,0],[4000,0],[4000,4000],[0,4000]]}',
    'roof': 'roof {"boundary":[[0,0],[4000,0],[4000,4000],[0,4000]]}',
    'ceiling': 'ceiling {"boundary":[[0,0],[4000,0],[4000,4000],[0,4000]]}',
    'door': 'door {"wall":"W","offset":1500}',
    'window': 'window {"wall":"W","offset":4000}',
    'railing': 'railing {"path":[[0,1000],[3000,1000]]}',
    'column': 'column {"at":[8000,8000]}',
    'structuralcolumn': 'structural_column {"at":[9000,9000]}',
    'footing': 'footing {"at":[10000,10000]}',
    'beam': 'beam {"points":[[0,20000],[5000,20000]]}',
    'stripfooting': 'strip_footing {"points":[[0,21000],[5000,21000]]}',
    'pipe': 'pipe {"points":[[0,22000],[5000,22000]]}',
    'duct': 'duct {"points":[[0,23000],[5000,23000]]}',
    'conduit': 'conduit {"points":[[0,24000],[5000,24000]]}',
    'cabletray': 'cable_tray {"points":[[0,25000],[5000,25000]]}',
    'wire': 'wire {"points":[[0,26000],[5000,26000]]}',
    'downconductor': 'down_conductor {"points":[[0,27000],[5000,27000]]}',
    'groundconductor': 'ground_conductor {"points":[[0,28000],[5000,28000]]}',
    'cable': 'cabling {"points":[[0,29000],[5000,29000]]}',
}
setup = sys.argv[1:]
cats = os.environ.get('CATS', ' '.join(place)).split()
res = {}
for cat in cats:
    tmp = tempfile.mkdtemp()
    cmds = list(setup)
    if cat in ('door', 'window'):
        cmds.append('wall {"points":[[0,0],[6000,0]],"type":"%s"}' % os.environ.get('HOSTWALL', 'Generic - 200mm'))
    cmds.append(place[cat].replace('"W"', '"LASTWALL"'))
    args = []
    for c in cmds:
        args += ['--cmd', c]
    # we need the wall id for doors: run once to learn it
    if cat in ('door', 'window'):
        r = subprocess.run([EXE, 'run'] + args[:-2], cwd=tmp, capture_output=True)
        lines = r.stdout.decode().strip().split('\n')
        wid = json.loads(lines[-1])['ids'][0]
        args[-1] = args[-1].replace('"LASTWALL"', str(wid))
    args += ['--save', 'x.bimcraft']
    r = subprocess.run([EXE, 'run'] + args, cwd=tmp, capture_output=True)
    if r.returncode:
        res[cat] = 'ERR ' + r.stderr.decode().strip()[-200:]
    else:
        d = json.load(open(os.path.join(tmp, 'x.bimcraft')))
        lib = {v['guid']: v['name'] for v in d['library'].values()}
        els = [e for e in d['elements'].values() if e.get('category') == cat]
        res[cat] = lib.get(els[-1].get('type'), els[-1].get('type')) if els else '??'
    shutil.rmtree(tmp)
for c in cats:
    print('%-16s %s' % (c, res[c]))

input.content:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Build the AREI symbol set data for src/structure/symbols/data.rs from the original's own output:
one project per name language, saved after `symbol_set {set: arei, names: <lang>}`."""
import json, subprocess, tempfile, os, shutil, sys

EXE = '/workspace/executable'
OUT = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else '/tmp/types-agent/data.rs'


def load(lang):
    tmp = tempfile.mkdtemp()
    r = subprocess.run([EXE, 'run', '--cmd', 'symbol_set {"set":"arei","names":"%s"}' % lang, '--save', 'x.bimcraft'],
                       cwd=tmp, capture_output=True, check=True)
    reply = json.loads(r.stdout.decode().strip().split('\n')[0])
    d = json.load(open(os.path.join(tmp, 'x.bimcraft')))
    shutil.rmtree(tmp)
    return reply, d


def base_families():
    tmp = tempfile.mkdtemp()
    subprocess.run([EXE, 'run', '--cmd', 'new {}', '--save', 'x.bimcraft'], cwd=tmp, capture_output=True, check=True)
    d = json.load(open(os.path.join(tmp, 'x.bimcraft')))
    shutil.rmtree(tmp)
    return set(d['families'])


base = base_families()
data = {}
for lang in ['en', 'nl', 'fr']:
    reply, d = load(lang)
    fams = {}
    for name in reply['loaded']:
        f = d['families'][name]
        assert name not in base
        assert f['parameters'] == [] and f['types'] == {'Standard': {}} and f['forms'] == [], name
        assert list(f.keys()) == ['category', 'parameters', 'types', 'forms', 'symbols'], (name, list(f.keys()))
        syms = []
        for s in f['symbols']:
            assert list(s.keys())[:2] == ['id', 'guid']
            syms.append({k: v for k, v in s.items() if k not in ('id', 'guid')})
        fams[name] = (f['category'], syms)
    data[lang] = (reply['loaded'], fams)

en_order, en = data['en']
key = lambda c_s: json.dumps(c_s, sort_keys=False)
by_geom = {}
for lang in ['nl', 'fr']:
    order, fams = data[lang]
    m = {}
    for n, cs in fams.items():
        k = key(cs)
        assert k not in m
        m[k] = n
    by_geom[lang] = (order, m)

rows = []
for i, n in enumerate(en_order):
    cs = en[n]
    k = key(cs)
    nl = by_geom['nl'][1][k]
    fr = by_geom['fr'][1][k]
    # the reply lists them in the data's order whatever the language
    assert by_geom['nl'][0][i] == nl and by_geom['fr'][0][i] == fr, (i, n, nl, fr)
    rows.append([n, nl, fr, cs[0], cs[1]])

text = json.dumps(rows, ensure_ascii=False, separators=(',', ':'))
# check that -0.0 survived
assert '-0.0' in text
with open(OUT, 'w') as f:
    f.write('//! The AREI/RGIE symbol set (Table 2.23): each family\'s English, Dutch and French names, its\n')
    f.write('//! category and its symbols in the family `symbols` schema, in the set\'s own order.\n')
    f.write('//! Generated; one row per family: [en, nl, fr, category, symbols].\n\n')
    f.write('pub const AREI: &str = r####"')
    f.write(text)
    f.write('"####;\n')
print('rows', len(rows), 'bytes', len(text))

"""Regression: run many cases through cmp.py (original vs mine), report failures.
usage: reg.py CASEFILE [-v] [-k substring]
A case file holds one case per line: commands separated by ' ;; ' (each `ID {json}`), optionally
prefixed by '@file.bimcraft ' to open a prepared input (from /tmp/types-agent/inputs/).
Every case ends with --save out.bimcraft and `inspect {}` is NOT added (add it yourself)."""
import subprocess, sys, os, shlex
MINE = os.environ.get('MINE', '/workspace/.claude/worktrees/agent-a7400d716490ebdc5/target/release/bimcraft-cli')
INPUTS = '/tmp/types-agent/inputs'
args = sys.argv[1:]
verbose = '-v' in args
key = None
if '-k' in args:
    key = args[args.index('-k') + 1]
files = [a for a in args if a.endswith('.txt')]
cases = []
for f in files:
    for line in open(f, encoding='utf-8'):
        line = line.rstrip('\n')
        if not line.strip() or line.startswith('#'):
            continue
        cases.append(line)
fails = []
for c in cases:
    if key and key not in c:
        continue
    fileargs = []
    runargs = ['run']
    if c.startswith('@'):
        fn, c2 = c[1:].split(' ', 1)
        fileargs = ['-f', os.path.join(INPUTS, fn)]
        runargs.append(fn)
        c = c2
    for cmd in c.split(' ;; '):
        runargs += ['--cmd', cmd]
    runargs += ['--save', 'out.bimcraft']
    r = subprocess.run(['python3', '/tmp/tools/cmp.py'] + fileargs + ['--'] + runargs,
                       capture_output=True, env=dict(os.environ, MINE=MINE), timeout=300)
    out = r.stdout.decode('utf-8', 'replace')
    ok = out.strip().endswith('SAME')
    if not ok:
        fails.append((c, out))
        if verbose:
            print('FAIL:', c[:300])
            print(out[:3000])
n = len([c for c in cases if not key or key in c])
print('%d/%d same' % (n - len(fails), n))
if not verbose:
    for c, out in fails:
        print('FAIL:', c[:200])

I've implemented `type` (Edit Type) and `symbol_set` in my own files and committed them on branch `worktree-agent-a7400d716490ebdc5` (head `cc25e4b`, 5 commits from `173d3cd`). Outside a few cases that depend on other areas, our output matches the original in everything I tested. I wrote no stand-ins for other areas.

**Test results** (scripts and cases in `/tmp/types-agent/`, `run_all.py` runs them all)
- **`type`**: 465/469 cmp.py cases match: errors and their order, every category's create/read/edit, layers, round toggling, GUID params, undo/redo. A random fuzzer also matched in 1200/1200 cases over three seeds, including a project with layered types.
  - 3 of the 4 differences are ARCH's door/window rules (a door or window that no longer fits or overlaps after a type edit).
  - The 4th is a loader issue: the original fills type defaults when it opens a file.
- **`symbol_set`**: 56/56. That covers all 76 families in en/nl/fr, the default by project language (a Dutch project gets Dutch, French gets French, others English), loading twice, en then nl, families already in the project, every error, and the undo label.
- **Default types**: 8/8 after renames and deletes, through our member commands.
- **Ids and GUIDs**: 35/35 for layer ids across undo, explicit ids and ids that clash.
- **Model rules**: 243/245 messages match on hand-edited projects. The 2 others are material GUIDs the library doesn't have, which the original's loader and material rules handle, not the type rules.
- **Undo history**: 8/8. **`types_view` against the original's `inspect` types**: 16/16 projects.

**Behaviour worth knowing**
- **Errors**: unknown keys and keys that don't apply to the category are ignored, and layers without a structure layer are accepted; there are no errors for these. Sizes that are zero, negative or out of range are refused by the type rules, not by the command, and those rules also run after every command. Refusals longer than 2000 characters are cut, as the original does.
- **Undo**: every successful `type` and `symbol_set` makes an undo step, even when nothing changed ("Edit Type", "Load Symbol Set"). Editing a type changes nothing else; walls keep their location line.
- **Wall layers**: a new `thickness` on a layered type goes to the first structure layer, or the thickest layer if none is structure. Replaced layers keep their old ids and GUIDs by position.
- **Material checks**: `types::check` doesn't check materials, because the original's loader creates any missing material a file names. The `type` command does check them.
- **Low layer ids**: the original's id counting with layer ids below 900000 is reproduced only inside `type`. The shared `alloc_lib_id` ignores such ids, so later commands may number differently. This only happens if a user gives layers such ids explicitly.

**Layer layout (for ARCH)**
- **Wall layers**: in `types.wall[name]` = `{thickness, layers?}`, ordered from the exterior side inward.
- **Floor, roof and ceiling layers**: ordered from the top down. The ceiling type is `{thickness, grid, layers?}`.
- **Each layer**: `{id, guid, function, material (GUID or ""), thickness, variable (only when true)}`.
- **Type thickness**: the sum of the layers (within 1e-6). The core runs from the first structure layer to the last.
- **`variable`**: only floors and roofs may have it, at most one layer.

**Public functions for other areas** (`src/structure/types.rs`, `src/structure/symbols/mod.rs`)
- `types::default_type(pr: &Project, cat: &str) -> Option<String>`: the category's named default if the project has it, otherwise the first type by byte order. This is the same in every project language, and a renamed or deleted default stops being the default. `types::default_name(cat) -> Option<&'static str>` gives the names.
- `types::layered(pr, cat, name) -> Option<(f64, Vec<Layer>)>`: thickness and layers with materials by name; `types::core(&[Layer]) -> Option<(f64, f64)>` gives the core's offsets from the exterior/top face. `types::spec_of(pr, cat, name) -> Option<Spec>` covers any category.
- `types::types_view(pr) -> Value` and `types::type_view(pr, cat, name) -> Option<Value>`: `inspect`'s `types` exactly (for READERS).
- `types::names_for_guids(pr, &params) -> Value`: the original replaces any string that is a library entry's GUID with that entry's name before reading params, including nested ones. Element GUIDs are left alone. Other areas probably need this too.
- `types::category_key(s) -> String`, `types::put_sorted(map, k, v)`, `types::clip(e)`, `types::check(pr)`, `symbols::arei()`.

**What other areas need to provide**
- **READERS (loader)**: on open the original
  - fills type defaults: sill 0, grid 0, spacing 0, round false;
  - sorts types, run categories and families by name;
  - drops library entries for types that no longer exist;
  - creates materials that types name but the library lacks;
  - requires the wall, floor, door and window type sections;
  - runs the model check, refusing with "open: <path>: <msg>".
- **ARCH**: the door/window fit rules. They decide the last 3 failing `type` cases.
